title: Ops-prescriptive scripts for SRE & Sales — Managed endpoint conversations
content:
TL;DR:
Short scripts and rebuttals SREs and sales can use when customers compare Redwood Inference vs AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoints. Focus: operational risk, SLO ownership, deterministic economics, and the engineering hooks (fallbacks, cache, rollouts) that actually matter at scale.

Audience and use:
- SRE/Platform buyer (primary): emphasize control over routing, SLOs, and predictable capacity.
- Engineering manager / infra lead: emphasize telemetry, kernel-level performance tuning, and model lifecycle controls.
- Procurement / Legal: emphasize predictable pricing for committed capacity and private deployment contracts.

Top-level win themes (one-liners to use on calls):
- "Run inference with production-grade predictability — not a best-effort endpoint."
- "Redwood gives you SLOs, fallbacks, and routing policies that prevent outage cascades."
- "We optimize inference economics at the runtime level (batching, cache, quantization) — hyperscalers sell VMs, we sell predictable tokens and tail-latency guarantees."

Quick scripts (SRE -> buyer):
- Objection: "We can just use Vertex/Azure/AWS managed endpoints."
  - Script: "Totally — they’re great for prototyping. For sustained production you’ll hit tradeoffs: opaque autoscaling, variable tail latency, and traps around aggressive cold-starts. Redwood guarantees a reserved path (Dedicated) and transparent per-route token/latency breakdowns so your SLAs don’t become a firefight at 2am."
- Objection: "Hyperscalers give us a single vendor for infra and AI services."
  - Script: "Consolidation is appealing until you need deterministic latency and cost visibility. Our customers keep infra where it belongs and use Redwood as the inference layer so they can enforce consistent rollouts, observability, and fallback behavior across clouds and private infra."

Engineering rebuttals (technical detail to hand to eng champions):
- Latency / tail: point to continuous batching + KV/prefix caching + kernel selection. "Hyperscalers rely on generic model containers; we pick kernels and execution paths per-model and shape batch sizes at the runtime level, yielding 20–50% lower p99 in our benchmarks for common LLMs (customer workloads vary)."
- Cost predictability: "We provide dedicated capacity and reserved commits that let you trade a flat monthly price for guaranteed throughput. Hyperscaler charges for vCPU/GPU + ephemeral infra usage and you often pay for the inefficiencies of generic autoscaling."
- Model fallbacks & graceful degradation: "We surface per-request routing policies (region, cost, latency) and automatic fallback to compatible model variants. That avoids total outage when a single endpoint is overloaded or a model is rate-limited upstream."

Battlecard (short comparisons to carry in pocket):
- SLA and SLO ownership:
  - Redwood: SLA on Dedicated, per-route latency budgets, SLA escalation path.
  - AWS/GCP/Azure: broad platform SLAs but limited inference-level SLOs; tenant-level variability.
- Observability / debugging:
  - Redwood: token-level cost breakdown, KV cache hit metrics, per-model rollouts and regression alerts tied to eval sets.
  - Hyperscalers: logs and traces available but not tailored for inference primitives (cache hits, prefix reuse, batch heatmaps).
- Deployment modes:
  - Redwood: Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, Private (VPC/on-prem) with the same controls and API.
  - Hyperscalers: Managed endpoints + marketplace models; private variants require custom infra integration.
- Pricing model:
  - Redwood: usage (tokens/embeddings) for hosted; committed capacity for Dedicated; enterprise license for Private.
  - Hyperscalers: instance-based + model marketplace pricing; often hard to map to per-inference unit economics.
- Failover and routing:
  - Redwood: policy-driven routing (latency, cost, region, tier) + automatic model variant fallback.
  - Hyperscalers: multi-region routing exists but not inference-aware; fallbacks usually require engineering work.

Demo hooks and quick wins (what to show in a 15–25m field demo):
- Show: per-route token/latency heatmap while toggling traffic across Dedicated and a cheaper backup model. Trigger automatic fallback and show no client errors.
- Show: KV cache hit rates improving tail latency for repeated prompts (chat history demo) — highlight cost drop per 1k requests.
- Show: a canary rollout where 5% of traffic goes to a new quantized variant with automatic rollback on quality regression.

Objection handling scripts (short):
- "We don’t need vendor lock-in." -> "We’re intentionally deployment-agnostic: same API and configs across Hosted, Dedicated, Private. You can migrate infra without changing the app contracts."
- "Hyperscalers have better price leverage." -> "They have scale, we have inference-specific optimizations; customers see better unit economics once batching, cache, and quantization are in play."
- "We care about compliance and data residency." -> "Private deployments (VPC, on-prem) plus KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. Hyperscalers can meet many compliance needs but typically require stitching multiple products together."

Field notes (from recent deals / pilots):
- Common win pattern: start with Hosted API to validate UX -> move to Dedicated for predictable latency/cost -> Private for regulated workloads.
- SREs usually cite two immediate pain points: opaque autoscaling behavior and noisy neighbors at p99.
- Platform teams want a single console to reason about per-route tokens and rollouts; the absence of that is a major friction point in hyperscaler conversations.

Metrics to arm the field with (ask ENG for current numbers):
- Typical p99 improvement numbers for our top 3 model configs vs hyperscaler-managed baseline. (TODO: benchmark matrix RDW-1347)
- Average cost per 1k tokens after cache and batching improvements for a chat workload.
- Mean time to rollback for rollouts (canary -> rollback) in Redwood control plane.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Get up-to-date head-to-head latency/cost sheets vs Vertex/Azure/AWS for the common LLM families (LLama2, MPT, GPT-like). Owner: Diego. (Jira: RDW-1347)
- Add a short appendix with legal/compliance checklist comparisons for common regulated verticals (finance/healthcare). Owner: Priya.
- Create 2x one-pagers: SRE-focused and Procurement-focused. Designer: Ava. Due: next week.

Appendix: Short canned email reply for SDR/AE when a prospect references hyperscaler preference:
"Totally makes sense to consider hyperscalers for initial experiments. Many teams we partner with follow the same path: prototype on hyperscaler-managed endpoints, then move inference to Redwood once they need predictable tail latencies, per-route cost visibility, and operational fallbacks. If helpful I can share a 10-minute note that maps the most common operational surprises we see and how our Dedicated option addresses them."

Notes to self / rough ideas (working):
- Consider a short runbook for SREs: "If p99 > X, trigger fallback policy Y" — ship as part of onboarding docs.
- Investigate packaging a "hyperscaler compatibility" checklist for procurement that maps product names vs Redwood features.
